title: Given an m by n grid of non-negative costs, find a path from top-left to bottom-right that minimizes the sum of costs, moving only right or down.
shortTitle: Minimum Path Sum — cheapest path through a weighted grid

s1_definition.profdef: Grid DP where dp[i][j] is the minimum cost to reach cell (i,j). The first row and column are prefix sums (only one way to reach them), and dp[i][j] = grid[i][j] + min(dp[i−1][j], dp[i][j−1]). Time O(m·n), space O(n) with a rolling row.
s1_definition.analogy: A funds-routing engine at National Bank of India sends money across a grid of correspondent banks, each hop charging a fee, moving only east or south. The cheapest way to reach any bank is its own fee plus the cheaper of arriving from the west or the north.
s1_definition.oneliner: dp[i][j] = cost + min(from above, from left).
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Grid DP where dp[i][j] is the minimum cost to reach cell (i,j). The first row and column are prefix sums (only one way to reach them), and dp[i][j] = grid[i][j] + min(dp[i−1][j], dp[i][j−1]). Time O(m·n), space O(n) with a rolling row.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** A funds-routing engine at National Bank of India sends money across a grid of correspondent banks, each hop charging a fee, moving only east or south. The cheapest way to reach any bank is its own fee plus the cheaper of arriving from the west or the north.

**One line to remember:** dp[i][j] = cost + min(from above, from left).

sections.s2_technical:
Create a dp grid of the same size. The top-left cell equals its own cost. The first row is a running sum because the only way along the top is to keep moving right, and the first column is a running sum because the only way down the left is to keep moving down. These are the base cases.

For each interior cell, add the cell's own cost to the cheaper of the cell above and the cell to the left: `dp[i][j] = grid[i][j] + Math.min(dp[i-1][j], dp[i][j-1]);`. The answer is the bottom-right cell dp[m−1][n−1].

The time and space are O(m·n), and space reduces to O(n) with a rolling row, or you can overwrite the input grid in place for O(1) extra space. A senior nuance is that because all costs are non-negative this simple DP suffices, but if negative costs or arbitrary moves were allowed you would need a shortest-path algorithm like Dijkstra instead.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — At National Bank of India, a funds-routing engine passes money through a grid of correspondent banks, each charging a fee, moving only east or south, and must pick the cheapest route. This is exactly how Minimum Path Sum works.

Problem 2 — Greedily taking the locally cheaper next hop can miss a better overall route. This is exactly why DP computes the true minimum cost to every cell.

The mini-project builds a `FundsRouter`, a `BankLogFormatter`, and a runnable demo.

sections.s5_journey:
The input grid of fees is one, three, one across the top, one, five, one in the middle, and four, two, one at the bottom.

Step 1: The top-left cell is one, the top row becomes running sums one, four, five, and the left column becomes one, two, six.

Step 2: The middle cell at row one column one is five plus the cheaper of four above or two to the left, giving seven.

Step 3: Interior cells each add their own fee to the cheaper incoming neighbor.

Step 4: The bottom-right cell adds its fee of one to the cheaper neighbor leading to seven.

Step 5: The cheapest total is seven along the route one, three, one, one, one.

sections.s6_takeaway:
Minimum Path Sum is a grid dynamic programming problem. I define dp of i and j as the minimum total cost to reach cell i, j moving only right or down. The base cases are the first row and first column, which are prefix sums because along an edge there is only one way to arrive, so the cost simply accumulates.

For every interior cell I add its own cost to the cheaper of the two ways to enter it, which is the minimum of the cell above and the cell to the left. The answer is the bottom-right cell. I can reduce the memory to a rolling row, or even overwrite the input grid in place for constant extra space.

In my project at National Bank of India, a funds-routing engine passed money through a grid of correspondent banks, each charging a fee, moving only east or south, and had to pick the cheapest route. A greedy next-cheapest-hop choice can miss a better overall route, so I used this DP that computes the true minimum to every cell. I also note that because all fees are non-negative this simple DP is enough, whereas negative costs or free movement would require a shortest-path algorithm like Dijkstra.
